Analog electronics · Optical sensing · Cadence/PSpice

Detecting Short Laser Pulses in Ambient Light: Filtering, Feedback and Signal Conditioning

Designing and simulating an optical receiver that distinguishes brief laser pulses from ambient-light disturbances and produces a clean 0–5 V logic signal.

Detecting a brief optical pulse becomes challenging when a sensor is also exposed to daylight and artificial lighting. In this laboratory project, a phototransistor was modeled as a current source, and several analog signal-processing architectures were evaluated in Cadence/PSpice to isolate the useful laser pulse.

Engineering objective

Reject slowly varying optical disturbances, preserve short laser events, and deliver a robust binary indication of laser presence — including when the useful signal is weak.

100 HzArtificial-light disturbance
0–5 VRequired output range
×20Gain for weak-pulse recovery

Modeling the optical environment

The sensor current was assembled from three components: a DC contribution representing ambient light, a 100 Hz sinusoidal contribution representing artificial illumination, and a short pulse representing the laser. This separation allowed the team to test how the receiver responds to both useful events and optical interference.

Sensor current model
isensor(t) = IM + iN(t) + ilaser(t)

The model superimposes ambient light IM, periodic disturbance iN, and the laser pulse ilaser. The exact waveform parameters are configured in the original simulation schematic.

Separating laser pulses from low-frequency noise

The baseline receiver used complementary filtering paths before signal conditioning. The report describes a high-pass path designed to reject frequencies below approximately 500 Hz, including DC and the 100 Hz lighting disturbance, alongside a low-pass branch whose contribution is combined through a summing stage.

The resulting filtered waveform made the short laser events more distinguishable from the slower background fluctuations.

First-order filter fundamentals
fc = 1 / (2πRC)
HHP(s) = sRC / (1 + sRC)
HLP(s) = 1 / (1 + sRC)

These are the standard first-order high-pass and low-pass expressions, provided as theoretical context. The report does not give a complete derivation of the combined filtering transfer function, so the overall circuit is not reduced to an unsupported single-filter model.

Converting an analog pulse into a logic signal

The conditioning stage combined an operational-amplifier hysteresis comparator and a level-shifting amplifier. Hysteresis prevents repeated switching when a noisy signal fluctuates near the decision threshold. The second stage maps the comparator output into the specified 0–5 V range.

Hysteresis width
ΔVH = VH+ − VH−

The report's component calculations use VH− = 0.75 V and VH+ = 3.5 V, yielding ΔVH = 2.75 V. From its resistor-ratio relation, it obtains R7 = 7.7 kΩ with R8 = 1 kΩ, and E1 = 2.9 V.

The introductory description elsewhere in the report mentions nominal thresholds of 1 V and 3 V. The numerical design calculation instead uses 0.75 V and 3.5 V; these are reported separately rather than presented as identical values.

Investigating the zero-ambient-light case

The team compared simulations with IM = 1 mA and IM = 0. Without the DC ambient component, the modeled current could become negative and the corresponding processed voltage could also cross below zero. The report identifies this as a problem for downstream conditioning stages designed around positive signals.

An added DC offset was therefore proposed to keep the processed signal in the operating range expected by the conditioning circuit. In a physical phototransistor, a negative optical photocurrent caused solely by removing illumination would not be interpreted literally; this observation concerns the report's superimposed-source simulation model.

Adding feedback to suppress ambient disturbances

The second architecture introduced a subtractor-based feedback path ahead of the filters. The subtractor formed a corrected signal from the phototransistor output and a returned signal. In the simulations, this reduced slow fluctuations and improved the visibility of the fast laser pulses.

Feedback subtraction
Vcorrected(t) = Vmeasured(t) − Vfeedback(t)

This is the functional relation implemented by the subtractor. The degree of disturbance cancellation depends on the actual feedback network and signal matching.

The report describes a more stable filtered signal and a logic output that detects the laser pulses similarly across the tested ambient-light conditions.

Implementing feedback with a bipolar transistor

A third variant added an NPN bipolar transistor that influences the phototransistor's operating point. This provides a more direct hardware feedback mechanism to oppose unwanted slow variations while preserving the short laser response.

The resulting PSpice waveforms showed a better-defined useful signal and a reliable conditioned output in the tested scenarios.

Recovering a very weak laser signal

Finally, the report reduced the useful laser-current amplitude to I₂ = 0.05 mA. With the original amplification, some pulses did not reach the hysteresis comparator's thresholds, resulting in missed detections at the output.

Increasing the gain of the amplification stage immediately before conditioning to 20 restored sufficient pulse amplitude. In the reported simulation, the missing pulses reappeared both before and after conditioning.

Signal amplification
Vout = Av Vin

For the final weak-signal simulation, the chosen gain was Av = 20. Amplification can restore threshold crossings, but it must be balanced against noise amplification and output saturation in a physical implementation.

Engineering takeaway

The study demonstrates an analog detection chain built around optical sensing, frequency-selective filtering, hysteresis-based decision making and feedback. Its central lesson is that filtering alone is not enough: the receiver must also maintain appropriate operating points and signal amplitude across changing lighting conditions.

Key result

With transistor-assisted feedback and a gain of 20, the simulated receiver recovered laser pulses at 0.05 mA that were missed at the original gain, while retaining a conditioned 0–5 V output.

All outcomes are based on idealized Cadence/PSpice simulations. The report does not present a fabricated prototype or measured optical detection probabilities.

Original laboratory report: Anaïs Sallard · Erwin Dumontel — ESIEE Paris, 2025–2026.
